units.text: The Guide and the Road After the Cave
How did trust relate to the guide’s expertise, and what can we say about the companions and the route without drawing a map the text does not provide?

When the time came to resume travel from the cave of Thawr, the two mounts were with a man whom the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr had hired for his knowledge of the route. We read why they trusted his expertise, when they had agreed to meet, who set off with them, and what the phrase “the coastal route” allows us to say. In another account, the word “guides” raises an important question: was Abu Bakr referring to the route guide when answering a question about his companion?
The Two Mounts in the Guide’s Care
The Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hired a man of Banu al-Dil, of Banu ‘Abd ibn ‘Adi, to guide them along the road. ‘A’isha describes him as “a skilled guide,” that is, an expert in finding the way.
The man followed the religion of the unbelievers of Quraysh. Nevertheless, they trusted him, entrusted their two mounts to him, and arranged a meeting with him.
The Meeting and Departure
They were to meet at the cave of Thawr after three nights. The guide came with the two mounts on the morning of the third day, as ‘A’isha relates.
‘Amir ibn Fuhayra and the guide set off with the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, and the guide took them along the coastal route.
Abu Bakr’s Answer

In Anas’s account of the Prophet’s approach to Medina ﷺ, people recognized Abu Bakr and asked him who the man with him was. He replied, “This man guides me along the way.” The listener thought he meant the road, but Abu Bakr meant the way of goodness.
The Guide’s Name: Who Named Him and Who Did Not?

The hiring passage in al-Bukhari does not give the guide’s personal name; it gives his lineage and expertise. In the Sira excerpt, Ibn Ishaq transmits Asma bint Abi Bakr’s list of four: the Prophet ﷺ, Abu Bakr, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayra, and ‘Abd Allah ibn Arqat, their guide. Ibn Hisham then adds another spelling with the formula “it is also said”: ‘Abd Allah ibn Urayqit. A tentative formulation cannot become a certainty; the different spelling alone does not imply two guides.

Asma’s excerpt begins “When we heard his words.” These words refer back to an account of a voice and poetry in the preceding Sira excerpt. We read them to understand the opening, not to establish the reported mysterious voice as a fact or authenticate the poem. The list in this excerpt is attributed to Asma as transmitted by Ibn Ishaq; the name is not extracted from al-Bukhari’s wording.

In a later commentary, Hani Faqih quotes a passage from Ibn Kathir naming him ‘Abd Allah ibn Urayqit. Hani then explains in his own voice that the report in the Sahih does not state the name and that Ibn Ishaq named him in the Sira. The quoted name and the commentator’s qualification are different voices: do not attribute Hani’s remark to Ibn Kathir, or take al-Bukhari’s silence as a denial of names in other works.
Report and Inference

In ‘A’isha’s hadith, expertise, trust, and difference of religion appear together: the guide is described as skilled, then entrusted with the two mounts even though he followed the religion of the unbelievers of Quraysh. Al-Qurtubi quotes the account from al-Bukhari, then attributes to al-Muhallab the inference that polytheists may be trusted with secrets and property when they are known to be faithful and honorable, and to Ibn al-Mundhir the inference that they may be hired as road guides. These are views attributed to commentators, not further details ‘A’isha witnessed. Repetition of the report in a commentary does not by itself create an independent account.
What the Route Specifies and What It Leaves Open

The phrase “they arranged to meet him” on the hiring page is completed by “at the cave of Thawr after three nights” on the next page of the same hadith. “The morning of the third” gives the time in the account, not a precise clock time or a calendar date. Likewise, “the coastal route” describes their route here, not a list of stopping places or a line plotted with coordinates.

Al-Bayhaqi transmits another report from Abu Hurayra: its chain and main text begin on one page and its sentence continues on the next. In that continuation Abu Bakr’s answer about his companion is “A guide who guides me.” Anas’s report, by contrast, says “This man guides me along the way” and explains that the meaning is the way of goodness. We preserve each account’s wording and join the truncated page to its continuation, without confusing either answer with the hired guide’s role or treating the page division as two independent chains.

Ibn Ishaq’s text attributed to Asma names Arqat; Ibn Hisham then adds Urayqit with “it is also said.”
The two spellings alone do not establish two people or independent sources.

“The Prophet of God ﷺ approached Medina with Abu Bakr riding behind him. Abu Bakr was an older man whom people recognized, while the Prophet of God ﷺ was a young man whom they did not recognize. A man would encounter Abu Bakr and ask, ‘Abu Bakr, who is this man before you?’ He would reply, ‘This man guides me along the way.’ The listener thought he meant the road, but he meant the way of goodness. Abu Bakr turned and saw a horseman who had caught up with them. He said, ‘Messenger of God, a horseman has caught up with us!’ The Prophet of God ﷺ turned and said, ‘O God, throw him down!’ His horse threw him and then rose neighing. He said, ‘Prophet of God, command me to do whatever you wish.’ He replied, ‘Stay where you are; let no one else follow us.’ Early in the day he had fought against the Prophet of God ﷺ; by the end of the day he was guarding him. The Messenger of God ﷺ stopped beside the lava tract and sent for the Ansar. They came to the Prophet of God ﷺ, greeted the two men, and said, ‘Ride on, safe and obeyed.’ The Prophet of God ﷺ and Abu Bakr rode on, and the Ansar surrounded them with weapons. People in Medina said, ‘The Prophet of God has come! The Prophet of God ﷺ has come!’ They peered out, looking and saying, ‘The Prophet of God has come! The Prophet of God has come!’ He continued until he stopped beside Abu Ayyub’s house. While he was speaking to his family, ‘Abd Allah [the name breaks off at the excerpt boundary] heard of him.”
